```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(goedel)
```

## Syntax is not truth

`goedel` constructs first-order terms and formulas with a versioned wire format.
Variables, constants and functions are terms. Predicates, equality, logical
connectives and quantifiers are formulas. Names are ASCII identifiers, at most
64 bytes; a single expression has at most 1000 nodes and depth 64. Arity is
checked consistently within each expression and jointly within proofs/search.
The same function name is permitted to have a different arity in unrelated
expressions, since no global signature is silently assigned.

```{r}
x <- variable("x")
y <- variable("y")
f <- forall("y", predicate("P", list(x, y)))
free_variables(f)
bound_variables(f)
```

The binder in the next substitution must be renamed. Replacing the free `x`
with `y` does not allow the existing quantifier to capture it.

```{r}
g <- substitute_formula(f, "x", y)
serialize_record(g)
free_variables(g)
normalize(g)
```

Fresh variable names are deterministic: `v0`, `v1`, and so on, excluding names
already present in the input or replacement. Shadowed bindings are preserved.
Alpha normalization names bound variables in preorder while skipping free names.
It is a syntactic transformation, not a decision procedure for logical equivalence.

## Exact codes

The numbering `goedel-json-byte-v1` begins at one and repeatedly applies
`n = 256*n + b` to each canonical JSON byte. The leading one acts as a sentinel.
Uniqueness of base-256 expansion gives an injective encoding of the canonical
byte strings. This finite algorithm is not itself a proof of arithmetical
representability of a substitution function.

```{r}
numbering()
code <- encode(variable("x"))
code
serialize_record(decode(code))
fingerprint(variable("x"))
```

R uses native decimal-digit arithmetic. No floating-point conversion of a code
is allowed: keep codes as character strings even when their values are small.
Encoding is limited to 1024 bytes and decoding to 2500 decimal digits. Decoder
success checks the sentinel, canonical wire text and valid syntax. Invalid
inputs produce `goedel_error` with `INVALID_INPUT`; exhausted resource limits
produce `RESOURCE_LIMIT`.

## Finite proof checking and bounded search

The native calculus is a small natural-deduction fragment, not a complete
arithmetic proof system. A proof consists of explicit formulas, rule names and
one-based references to earlier steps. Axioms must be closed; supplied
assumptions and axioms remain trusted premises.

```{r}
a <- predicate("A")
b <- predicate("B")
assumptions <- list(a, implication(a, b))
steps <- list(
  list(rule = "assumption", formula = a, premises = list()),
  list(rule = "assumption", formula = implication(a, b), premises = list()),
  list(rule = "mp", formula = b, premises = list(1L, 2L))
)
check_proof(steps, assumptions, conclusion = b)
```

Supported rules are assumption, axiom, modus ponens, conjunction introduction,
left/right conjunction projection, universal elimination by capture-avoiding
substitution, and universal introduction with its free-variable side condition.
The original checker retains this small fragment; `check_scoped_proof()` adds
explicit discharged subproofs and the fuller rules described below.
A mutated rule application returns `REFUTED` about the validity of that submitted
proof, not about the truth of its conclusion. Malformed payloads are errors.

```{r}
steps[[3]]$formula <- a
check_proof(steps, assumptions)$details
found <- bounded_proof_search(b, assumptions)
found$details
check_proof(found$witness, assumptions)$status
bounded_proof_search(b, list(a))$details
```

Search closes a finite set only under modus ponens and conjunction projection.
Assumptions are inserted in order; facts are deduplicated modulo alpha-renaming.
The maximum budget is 256 admitted proof steps, including assumptions. A witness
is independently checked before success. `UNKNOWN` with `BOUND_EXHAUSTED` or
`SEARCH_SPACE_EXHAUSTED` says nothing about unbounded provability.

## Literature and conditional applicability

The public catalogue describes precise variants of metamathematical results.
The original Gödel sentences, Rosser's refinement, the second incompleteness
theorem, Löb's theorem and Tarski's undefinability theorem are distinct entries.
They are never interchanged merely because they concern truth or provability.
Their exact literature formulations, requirements and sources are data.

```{r}
list_statements()
rosser <- lookup_statement("rosser")
rosser$requirements
rosser$evidence$review_status
check_applicability("rosser", theory_context("PA"))$status
```

A name such as PA does not silently certify effectiveness, arithmetical strength
or consistency. Explicit declarations permit a conditional applicability query:

```{r}
declarations <- setNames(rep(list(TRUE), length(rosser$requirements)),
                         unlist(rosser$requirements))
context <- theory_context("declared theory", declarations)
answer <- check_applicability("rosser", context)
answer$status
answer$limitations
context$consistency_status
```

Missing requirements yield `UNKNOWN`; false requirements yield `NOT_APPLICABLE`.
Detected contradictory declarations yield `INCONSISTENT_CONTEXT`. There is no
complete consistency decision procedure. `DRAFT` records cannot be activated by
adding assumptions. Literature review is not a locally replayed formal proof.
The direct typed graph returned by `relation_graph()` never turns arbitrary paths
into theorems.

## Reproducibility and scope

Canonical JSON, exact codes, SHA-256 fingerprints, the catalogue and shared
reference fixtures are aligned with the native Python implementation. Independent
reference derivations test mathematical behavior; language parity alone does not
prove correctness. Both packages can be installed and used without the other.
The legacy byte numbering and proof API remain stable. The larger syntax and
proof capabilities have explicit limits and independent mathematical tests;
none carries a proof-assistant certification.

```{r}
catalogue_manifest()
```


## Q, PA and exact numeral notation

The arithmetic signature has zero, successor, addition, multiplication and
logical equality. `q_axioms()` returns seven closed Robinson axioms in a stable
order. `arithmetic_theory("PA")` uses these axioms and the induction schema;
the Q predecessor axiom is redundant in this PA presentation. Additional closed
arithmetic axioms remain declared assumptions, not proved extensions.

```{r}
pa <- arithmetic_theory("PA")
body <- parse_formula("x + y = y + x")
instance <- induction_axiom(body, "x")
format_formula(instance)
recognize_induction(instance)$parameters
is_axiom(pa, instance)
pa$consistency_status
```

The body uses the fixed arithmetic signature; arbitrary extra predicate symbols
are rejected. An open induction instance can be recognized, but axiom membership
requires its universal closure. Membership is an exact syntactic decision,
separate from testing whether an arbitrary formula is a theorem.

Numerals are canonical decimal strings, never rounded machine numbers. The
`num` node explicitly abbreviates a binary Horner term. In an arbitrary finite
structure it denotes exactly that term, rather than an assumed standard natural
number. Expansion remains subject to the AST resource bounds.

```{r}
numeral_value(multiply(numeral("123456789"), numeral("987654321")))
format_formula(expand_numeral(numeral("5")))
format_formula(parse_formula("@zero = 0")) # Distinct syntax, explicit abbreviation
```

## Discharged proofs and equality

The larger native calculus uses an explicit stack of local assumptions. Closing
rules discharge the most recently opened assumption, and no closed line can be
reused outside its scope. Actual local proof dependencies are reported. Universal
introduction checks all global and open local assumptions; existential elimination
also checks the eigenvariable against its existential premise and conclusion.

```{r}
a <- predicate("A")
scoped <- list(
  list(rule="assume", formula=a, premises=list(), scope=list(1L)),
  list(rule="imp_intro", formula=implication(a,a), premises=list(1L),
       scope=list(), discharge=list(1L))
)
check_scoped_proof(scoped)$dependencies
```

The checker also has equality reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity and explicit
capture-avoiding template substitution. Disjunction elimination uses A or B,
A implies C, and B implies C. The classical contradiction rule is rejected when
`logic="intuitionistic"`. Checking a submitted derivation certifies only the
native rule checks relative to the supplied axioms, not consistency or truth of
those axioms, and is not a formally verified proof.

## Explicit finite semantics

Every function and relation interpretation is a complete table. Relation tables
include false rows; missing interpretations never default to false, even in an
unvisited short-circuit branch. A model has at most sixteen elements. Evaluation
visits formula nodes and interpreted terms with an explicit step budget.

```{r}
model <- finite_structure(c("a", "b"))
evaluate_formula(parse_formula("forall x. x = x"), model)$details
counter <- evaluate_formula(parse_formula("forall x. forall y. x = y"), model)
counter$witness
finite_model_check(list(parse_formula("x = x")), model)$details
```

`finite_model_check()` ranges over all assignments to free variables for exactly
the supplied list of formulas. Finite satisfaction of a list is neither a model
of the entire PA schema nor a consistency argument for PA.

## Finite modal models and frames

Modal syntax is separate from first-order syntax. A Kripke model explicitly
specifies worlds, accessibility edges, and the complete valuation of every atom
used by the formula. Box and diamond use the usual all-successors and
some-successor clauses, including empty successor sets.

```{r}
p <- modal_atom("p")
model <- kripke_model(c("a", "b"), list(list("a", "b")), list(p=list("b")))
evaluate_modal(modal_box(p), model, "a")$details
frame_check(model)
t_axiom <- modal_implication(modal_box(p), p)
validate_modal_frame(t_axiom, list("a"), list())$witness
validate_modal_frame(t_axiom, list("a"), list(list("a", "a")))$status
```

Frame validation enumerates every valuation of the formula's finite atom set and
every world. If the complete space exceeds the declared resource bound, it raises
`RESOURCE_LIMIT` before making a validity claim. Finite modal validity never
stands for general GL completeness or arithmetic provability.

## Large arithmetic presentations and exact proof transport

Arithmetic DAGs share literal subexpressions while preserving lexical variable
binding. Their separately bounded profile does not weaken the ordinary syntax
limits. Each imported ASCII variable name receives an injective numeric index
from a leading sentinel byte and its ASCII bytes. Compiler-generated indexed
names are already in the DAG namespace. Expanded node counts use exact GMP
arithmetic, including when a small shared graph denotes an exponentially large
formula tree.

```{r}
dag <- arithmetic_dag(parse_formula("x = x"))
validate_arithmetic_dag(dag)
dag_code <- arithmetic_dag_encode(dag)
identical(arithmetic_dag_decode(dag_code), dag)
closed <- dag_substitute_numeral(dag, "x376", "12345678901234567890")
validate_arithmetic_dag(closed)
```

DAG numbering identifies the entire presentation, including unreachable and
repeated nodes. It does not quotient by alpha equivalence or equality of expanded
root formulas. Closed numeral substitution retains every original node and
appends its transformed copy; this exact code equation is part of the numbering
contract. General `dag_substitute()` also supports variable-containing terms and
renames conflicting binders to avoid capture.

The self-delimiting natural sequence code uses no floating-point intermediates.
The empty sequence is 1 and invalid code is 0. Explicit runtime limits on digits,
bits, items and nodes are separate from the underlying unbounded mathematical
coding functions.

```{r}
sequence_encode(list("0", "0"))
sequence_decode(sequence_encode(list("0", "1", "12345678901234567890")))
record <- proof_object(scoped)
proof_code <- encode_proof(record)
check_proof_code(proof_code)$status
```

A proof transport object binds its calculus, theory descriptor and theory hash.
Decoding validates identity and shape; replay checks inference rules. An invalid
but well-formed derivation can still be encoded. This JSON-byte transport is
explicitly distinct from an arithmetical Proof_T predicate; transporting a proof
object alone does not establish representability or derivability conditions.

## Concrete conditional fixed points

`fixed_point()` uses a concrete arithmetic formula compiled from the documented
closed-substitution register program. Every instruction is expanded into arithmetic
with beta-coded traces; no oracle atom called Sub is inserted. The returned
sentence G and exact codes satisfy the specified substitution-code equation.
The full graph is large, so this construction is intentionally not run while
building this introductory vignette.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
phi <- arithmetic_dag(parse_formula("x = 0"))
fixed <- fixed_point(phi)
fixed$details
fixed$witness$checked_proof$status
fixed$assumptions[[1]]$proved_by_native_checker # FALSE
```

The twenty-step first-order derivation verifies G if and only if phi(code(G))
relative to its displayed representation instance. The instance is supported by
an independent mathematical review bound to exact program, compiler and formula
hashes. It is an explicit trusted premise of the native checker. The result does
not assert G's truth, unprovability or consistency, and no formal proof assistant
kernel was replayed. An unrecognized bundle or altered review cannot obtain the
built-in reviewed status merely by setting a verification flag.

## Typed conditional catalogue inference

The inference engine follows reviewed typed rules with explicit theory and
metatheory identities. Here the declared omega-consistency of a PA extension
supports Sigma-1 soundness and consistency, which supplies one of Rosser's
requirements. The declarations themselves remain unverified.

```{r}
ctx <- inference_context("declared PA extension", list(
  classical_first_order=TRUE, extends_pa=TRUE, omega_consistent=TRUE,
  decidable_axiom_set=TRUE, standard_arithmetization=TRUE
))
result <- infer("syntactically_complete", FALSE, ctx)
result$status
check_derivation(result$witness)$status
vapply(explain_derivation(result$witness), function(step) step$explanation, "")
```

Witnesses bind the exact catalogue and rule hashes. Independent replay rejects
changed assumptions, polarity, rule references, theory level or predicate identity.
Graph edges remain typed: a prerequisite or proof dependency is not automatically
an implication. The optional `catalogue_graph("igraph")` adapter retains the
full records as canonical JSON; its mathematical content matches the plain-record
adapter and the Python graph adapter.

## The exact PA proof predicate and metatheorems

The package includes the complete finite Hilbert PA checker as an explicit
register program. Its arithmetic graph represents that same program. The
proof predicate fixes the graph output to one; existential quantification over
the proof code gives `provability_formula()`. The predicate identity binds the
program, arithmetic graph, numbering, calculus and literal contradiction code.
`consistency_formula()` constructs the negation of this particular predicate at
that contradiction code; it does not establish the resulting formula.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
axiom_code <- arithmetic_dag_encode(hilbert_q_axiom(4L))
proof_code <- pa_proof_encode(list(list(
  rule=14L, formula=axiom_code, aux_a="0", aux_b="0"
)))
check_pa_proof(proof_code, axiom_code)$status # ESTABLISHED
provability_identity()
check_metatheorem("godel_second_hbl", list(consistent=TRUE))$status
check_metatheorem("lob", list())$details$hbl_conditions
sentence <- godel_sentence()
sentence$details
```

These complete constructions and checks can take substantial time and memory.
Internal node and context counts do not bound memory in bytes or wall time.
Use a separate worker with operating-system memory and execution-time limits,
run substantial cases sequentially, and begin with a small formula. A terminated
worker provides no mathematical verdict; a full PA Goedel sentence may exceed
the available local budget.
Their native implementations are exercised separately from the introductory
vignette build. A rejected finite PA proof is distinct from exhaustion of its
execution budget. The actual Goedel sentence is the fixed point of the explicit
formula not Pr_PA(x), and retains the same displayed representation premise as
`fixed_point()`.

The D1, D2 and D3 schemes have an independent mathematical review for this exact
predicate. They are not a proof-assistant certificate or a replayed serialized
PA proof of the schemes. `check_metatheorem()` checks each named variant's
requirements separately. A consistency declaration remains an assumption;
missing requirements yield UNKNOWN, false mathematical requirements yield
NOT_APPLICABLE, and inconsistent declarations yield INCONSISTENT_CONTEXT.
Different predicate identities or missing derivability-condition reviews cannot
be repaired by setting user flags to TRUE.

Public representation specifications, source programs and compilers are installed
under `system.file("reproduction", package="goedel")`. They support independent
reconstruction and review of the arithmetic resources. Normal R evaluation and
proof checking use the native implementations and do not invoke Python or these
reference sources.
